Bontia is widespread throughout the islands of the Caribbean-Bahamas, Cuba, Turk and Caicos Islands, Hispaniola, Puerto Rico, Virgin Islands, Jamaica, Cayman and FLORIDA PUERTO JAMAICA "HAITI DOMINICAN REPUBLIC COLOMBIA VENEZUELA Swan Islands and the Lesser Antilles, including Antigua, Barbuda, Guadeloupe, Dominica, Martinique, St Lucia, St Vincent, Aruba and Caraca. Maps 1 (p. 59), 56. It is probably indigenous to parts of coastal Venezuela and Guyana. It has also been recorded from Barbados, the reputed type locality, but no recent collections other than cultivated ones have been made. It has very recently been recorded from near Miami, continental United States of America. The species is common in coastal shrublands, forest or on the margins of mangroves on sand, saline clays or on limestone where it is often the dominant shrub. Although it favours dry exposed sites it will tolerate relatively high rainfall and in Puerto Rico it grows in areas that receive annual rainfalls up to 1800 mm. Like the majority of Myoporacee it favours open sunny situations.

Although a specimen labelled Bontia daphnoides is held at LINN (Savage Catalogue No. 812.1), an examination showed it not to be this species. The vegetative specimen superficially resembles Bontia in the shape of the leaf but the few irregular marginal notches are inconsistent with serrations occasionally found in Bontia and the venation is quite different. In addition, branches and leaves are pubescent, clothed in simple crisped hairs with the leaf buds being especially hairy. Linnaeus adopted the generic name Bontia, which had been first used by Plumier (1703) and supplemented it with information from Dillenius's treatment (1732). He also indicated in symbol form that he had seen material and it is possible that it was the above-mentioned specimen. He also placed Plukenet's 1694) "Olea, sylvestris barbadensis' in synonymy, and presumably his reference to Barbados as the origin was taken from Plukenet. Dillenius provided a detailed description and illustration of Bontia and the illustration depicted a leafy branch with buds and analytical drawings of calyx, gynoecium and fruit. No Dillenius specimen is held at (see Clokie, account of Herbaria in OXF), but a copy of Dilleniuss 'Hortus Elthamensis' (1732) held at Friedrich Schiller University, Jena (JE), has been annotated throughout by Linnaeus (see H. Schmidt, Feddes Repert. Spec. Nov. Regni Veg. 70: 67--108), including the Bontia treatment. It was presumably used by Linnaeus to prepare his treatment for Genera Plantarum so it is selected as lectotype. It is presumed that Linnaeus misidentified the sterile specimen in the LINN herbarium. Gaertner (1791) recognised a second species B. minor, but from the description and illustrations of the fruit it appears that this was merely a smaller fruit ( immature form of B. daphnoides. This species is widely cultivated in the Caribbean as an ornamental or as a hedge or windbreak. It is quite salt tolerant.

Diocirea acutifolia is only known from the Coolgardie Botanical District in the areas north of Norseman. It grows abundantly in open Eucalyptus salmonophloia woodland with E. salubris, E. floctonide, Melaleuca and Atriplex on older leaves vesicaria on red-brown powdery to gravelly clay loams. It usually dominates the ground layer.

Diocirea acutifolia is readily distinguished from the other species by its larger spreading linear-subulate leaves. Apart from the presence of resin at the branch tips this species, when in the vegetative state, could easily be mistaken for a member of the Epacridaceae. This species exudes resin, which eventually dries to form a white coating on the branches and leaves. In most cases the whitish resin only occurs as scattered patches but occasionally the whole plant can appear glaucous due to a very even covering on the leaves (Kuchel 1790). The quantity of resin exuded may be related to the moisture received, with larger quantities of resin being exuded in drier periods to reduce water loss.

Eremophila adenotricha is known only from three localities in the Avon Botanical District, Western - Australia. It occurs in tall Eucalyptus woodlands over Melaleuca tall shrubland, often with Atriplex vesicaria and Dodonaea spp. At the locations where it has been observed, the species was abundant in disturbed sites along the road and on side tracks.

Two specimens are held at MEL but only one of these, collected by J. Drummond, was seen by Bentham. The Botanical Museum of Melbourne' label, two blue packages with plant fragments and a manuscript description all have Eremophila adenotricha written on them in Mueller's handwriting. There is no doubt that this is the holotype. Gardner noted on his collection label that E. adenotricha grew with Eucalyptus floctoniae in the Glenelg Hills but a search in 1977 failed to locate the species. In 1987, B.H. Smith discovered the species west of this area at Holeton and a subsequent visit by me in 1990 found the species to be abundant in a relatively small area. It occurred commonly in disturbed sites, often where vehicles had been off-road. Populations in these places numbered many hundreds and plants appeared to be of similar age. They were spindly with lower branches dying off and active growth only at the tips. The populations appeared to be only a few years old (probably 3--5). It seems likely that this species is relatively short-lived, favouring very open sites. Mollemans et al. (1993) estimated one population at 10,000 plants and were of the opinion that the species favoured disturbed sites where it regenerated abundantly for a short period before contracting again to very low numbers. Fruits were abundantly produced at all populations that I saw and many were observed lying on the ground or partially buried A good germination occurrence most probably occurs in such areas after soil disturbance or after fire opens up areas. This followed by favourable rains in the following autumn/winter would probably promote a large seedling storm as is the case with many species of Eremophila.

Eremophila arbuscula is easily mistaken for E. oppositifolia subsp. rubra as both have an appressed grey tomentum on the branches and leaves and oblanceolate sepals. However, E. arbuscula can be distinguished by its longer, soft, flexible, attenuated leaves with an unpleasant odour (when crushed) and its smaller sepals (less than 6 mm long) and flowers. It would appear that the main flowering period for this species is summer to early autumn compared with the late winter-spring period for most species. Visits made to the Grey Range over a number of years from September to early November failed to find any populations in flower. One plant cultivated in Adelaide has consistently commenced flowering in late November or early December, continuing through to at least early March. The type collection was made in mid-May from a small tree with only one large branch in flower while the rest of the population was not flowering (M.E. Ballingall, pers. comm.). There is one flowering specimen (Smith 6085) made in mid- November but there is no indication as to whether it was a general population flowering or merely a premature flowering of an individual.

Eremophila battii is widespread and scattered throughout South Australia and Western Australia and the extreme south-central part of the Northern Territory. This species occurs on red-brown sandy loams or clays often in areas subject to occasional flooding. It usually occurs in mulga woodland Eremophila battii and is frequently associated with chenopod shrubs and other species of Eremophila.

The type sheet held at MEL consists of seven portions of branch some of which possess flowers. In addition there is a package containing flowers, fruits and fragments of branches and leaves. There are two identical 'Phytologic Museum of Melbourne' labels on the sheet with 'Eremophila battii FvM, Eucla, 1890 D. Batt' in Mueller's handwriting and on another piece of paper with a description of various parts of the plant also in Muellers hand. This collection is more complete than the Kew specimen and in addition has additional notes made by Mueller so it is here selected as lectotype. The var. major described by J.M. Black is typical of the species and contrary to his description the corollas on the type sheet are quite hairy. The larger leaves to 20mm long are on the older parts of the stem and probably developed during active vegetative growth; however, leaves on the lateral branches are considerably smaller. Eremophila battii is closely allied to E. spinescens (see Notes under this species) but the short curved white hairs on vegetative parts also suggest a link with E. gilesii and allied species. The obtuse corolla lobes may also suggest a link to E. pallida and E. viscimarginata.

Eremophila behriana is endemic to South Australia, extending from Eyre Peninsula to Yorke Peninsula, Southern Lofty, Murray and Kangaroo Island Regions. It occurs on light brown sandy loams in Eucalyptus woodland or in open scrub and is frequently found on disturbed soils along Eremophila behriana roadsides and tracks. In these latter situations root-suckering is very common.

Eremophila behriana is closely allied to E. crassifolia, E gibbifolia and E. barbata but differs by the shape and serrations of the leaves, the prominently ciliate leaf and sepal margins and the obovoid fruit. In his discussion of a newly described species, Pholidia crassifolia, Ferdinand Mueller (1853) described P. behriana indirectly. However, in this latter case no details were provided in the protologue of either the collector or locality. Pholidia crassifolia had been collected by C. Wilhelmi at 'Dombey-bay' (presumably a misspelling of Tumby Bay) and there are also collections of P. behriana, which were also collected by Wilhelmi at this locality. It is reasonable to assume that Mueller had these collections at his disposal when describing P. crassifolia and therefore they have been interpreted as being the type material upon which he based his observations. In his report on the Babbage expedition (1859) Mueller used the name E. behrii, but it is quite clear from the description provided and the locations from which the species was known that this was a misspelling of E. bebriana.

Eremophila calorhabdos is widespread throughout the eastern part of the Roe Botanical District extending into adjacent portions of the Eyre and Coolgardie Botanical Districts. It occurs on light brown sandy clay loams or deep fine sands in open shrub-mallee associations especially in open situations. At one site 55 km E of Lake King (Chinnock 4152, 4153), a large population had developed in regenerating mallee that had been burnt one or two years earlier. The growth form was consistently of the 'rod' type with plants consisting of 1 or 2 erect unbranched stems 1.5--2 m tall. Plants were common throughout the burnt-over area and it appears that the large population was the result of a high seed germination following the fire. Further populations (Chinnock 5456, 7391) exhibiting the same growth form also occurred in areas fired recently, suggesting that this species, like many eremophilas, is a fire-response species. In other situations where this species has been observed the growth form was of the more branched 'non-rod' type; in these cases few plants were present and they were associated with disturbed soils on the margin of mallee or along roads and appeared to be quite old.

Eremophila calorhabdos is related to the E. glabra group of species. The flower and fruit conform but the peculiar growth habit is atypical although forms of E subfloccosa do approach it. The fruit structure most closely resembles E. biserrata and may suggest a relationship with that species. The corolla colour changes from orange-yellow at the bud stage to carmine when the corolla opens. Such marked colour changes from the bud stage to open flower are also seen in E. denticulata and E. racemosa.

Considerable leaf variation occurs in this species. In the commonest form the leaf is lanceolate with 1--3 pairs of prominent spreading or recurved teeth at the base and sometimes with a few obscure teeth near the apex. Domin's M. latisepalum was based on an oblanceolate leaf form lacking the basal teeth but with an obtuse apex with some teeth. The broadest leaf forms are found in this type. Flower colour also varies considerably, from white to lilac occasionally mauve (north of Chinchilla, Wilberforce). Allan (1961) in his description of the species in New Zealand refers to the flower colour as purplish, and living material studied at the Auckland Regional Authority Botanical Garden at Manurewa, presumably of New Zealand origin, had deep mauve flowers. Gardens, Manurewa, Auckland, New Zealand The New Zealand occurrence of this species is here treated as adventive. Allan (1961) first included E. debilis in the New Zealand flora, the species having been collected a few years earlier by R.O. Green on the coast between Kawhia and Raglan. Apparently Green found the species after following the directions of an elderly man over 80 years old who remembered seeing the plant in his boyhood. (P. de Lange, pers. comm.). Allan argued that because it was growing on a very remote part of the New Zealand coast it was unlikely that it was of garden origin. However, Mr P. de Lange (pers. comm.), who had made a study of the occurrence of this species in New Zealand and made extensive searches for it, is of the opinion, and I agree with him, that the species is an introduction. The reasons to support this are: 1. During the 1830s onwards there was a very active trade along this coast with Sydney and other Australian ports. 2. In this area there are also other odd Australian adventives, for example, Cassinia aculeata. 3. In 1977 J.K. Bartlett following R.O. Green's instructions tried to locate the original site and searched a gully between Papanuiti Point and Te Toto Gorge. He apparently did not locate the plant and mentioned evidence of recent fires. Given (1981) considered that fire may have wiped out the plant but I do not believe this as E. debilis is widespread in fire-prone areas in Australia and the well-developed tap-root with branches arising from its crown suggest that this species readily resprouts after fire. Peter de Lange visited the area and found numerous Australian plants in abundance, including Hakea salicifolia, H. gibbosa, Eucalyptus sp., Grevillea sp., Carex longibrachiata and others, on the cliffs abutting an old homestead 4. A population of 15 plants was found on a series of cliffs at Rengarenga Point in 1974. They were growing in pasture and scrub and according to Peter de Lange were very unhealthy and none survived beyond 1980. They appeared to have been planted and according to local knowledge (P. de Lange, pers. comm.) occurred in an area which equated with an old flour mill which ground wheat grown in the Oparau valley and then sold to Sydney. Artefacts in middens show that the inter-Tasman trade was well established in the 1830s. 5. The corolla colour found in plants cultivated in New Zealand is mauve (purplish according to Allan, 1961); however, in Australia the species normally has white flowers or white with a faint suggestion of lilac, and strongly-coloured forms are exceedingly rare in the wild. However, it is often these atypical forms that are selected for cultivation because of their more spectacular flowers. As Australian plants appeared to have be cultivated in areas along the Kawhia-Raglan coast which had an active trade with Australian ports it is likely that the more spectacularly-coloured flower forms of species would have been introduced by persons with an interest in Australian plants. Finally one cannot rule out the possibility that the introduction of E. debilis was accidental. It is quite conceivable that the species arrived in soil ballast discarded by a visiting ship to load grain for Sydney. Even if the ballast were discarded at sea the large fleshy fruits are quite capable of remaining afloat for more than 20 days, sufficient time for them to be washed ashore.

Eremophila deserti is extremely widespread throughout south-eastern Queensland, New South Wales, western Victoria, southern "•:. South Australia. It also occurs scattered through Western -in* Australia south of latitude 25°S but most frequently along the Eremophila deserti Nullarbor. E. deserti occurs on a large variety of soil types including dark grey cracking clays, black soils, dark brown clays, red-brown sandy loams, yellow-brown silty loam, heavy red soils, sandy clay loams over granites, deep yellow sands and red-brown sands and on dunes. Throughout south-eastern Australia E. deserti is commonly found in Eucalyptus woodlands but in Queensland it is just as common in brigalow scrub. Occasionally it occurs in Callitris woodland In South and Western Australia it is common in Eucalyptus (mallee) woodlands, myall (Acacia papyrocarpa) and cypress pine (Callitris spp.) woodlands, Melaleuca shrublands, chenopodiaceous (Maireanal Atriplex) low shrublands and even on poorly drained soils in Halosarcial Nitraria low shrubland.

Leaf shape and size are extremely variable in E. deserti, ranging from long linear attenuated forms through to oblanceolate, obtuse-leaved ones. Very short, often obtuse-leaved forms appear to be more common in exposed coastal areas like along the Eucla escarpment and adjacent coastal plain (Hj. Eichler 21333, AD) or on offshore islands (Franklin Island, SA, D.C. Howlett 4B, AD). Leaf width also varies considerably and although typically 3--6 mm wide, extremely narrow forms with widths 0.8--1 mm are occasionally encountered (J.B. Cleland s.n. AD97609564). Fruit colour is also quite variable and although typically yellow to brownish yellow it can range to yellow tinged purple to dark brownish purple. A form which occurs in north-eastern Australia along the Great Dividing Range was first described by Mueller (1865) as which dilate distally, and leaves which are thinner and appear discolorous, although the thinner leaves are probably a result of habitat as this form appears to be associated with woodlands, occurring in more shaded and sheltered situations. Although many specimens of this form appear to be very distinct, many gradations to the more typical forms exist and population studies will be necessary to determine whether there is any sound basis for recognition at an infraspecific level. Forms of Eremophila deserti are known to be poisonous to stock, and 11 toxic furanoid sesquiterpenes have been isolated (see Everist, 1981), however, other forms of this species appear non-toxic with no ill effect on browsing animals (Everist 1947). No correlation between plant form and toxicity has yet been determined so all forms of E. deserti should be treated as toxic.

Eremophila dichroantha is extremely uniform throughout its range. It is closely allied to E. interstans, E. dempsteri, E psilocaly and E. ciliata. It is readily distinguished from the former three species by the large tubercles found on the branches and leaves and the small tubular violet flowers, and from E. mm 2.5 ciliata by the linear-subterete leaves and the branches which do not become banded When Mueller (1876) referred to E. exiliflora in a discussion following the description of E. dempsteri he provided no description to identify this species. However, a specimen of E dichroantha in the Melbourne Herbarium, which has a label in Mueller's hand, has E. dempsteri var. exiliflora as his identification. This specimen was collected by Dempster between Esperance and Fraser's Range and there is little doubt that this was the plant referred to by Mueller. Eremophila drummondii is widespread and common throughout the Avon Botanical District and western parts of the Coolgardie and Roe Botanical Districts. It occurs on a variety of soil types including red and yellow earthy sands, red duplex soils and red and yellow non-calcareous earths. It usually occurs in Eucalyptus and mallee woodlands and Acacia shrublands on sandy plains.

Although the flower and fruit of Eremophila drummondii are relatively uniform over its range, considerable variation occurs in the shape of the leaf. Spencer Moore based his variety brevis on a form with rigid, erect, clustered leaves; however, this appears to be no more than an extreme which occurs sporadically along the drier northern edges of the species range. The broader oblanceolate leaf forms occur along the southern edges of this species distribution. E. drummondii is most closely allied to E. rugosa. It differs from that species in lacking hairs on the vegetative parts and pedicels, non-rugose branches and a glabrous corolla. It also has affinities with E. sargentii, differing in features of the branch, leaf arrangement, larger flowers and by having 2 ovules per locule. In addition it lacks the strong, often pungent odour characteristic of E. sargentii and related species.

Eremophila duttonii extends from the Warburton region of Western Australia through the Northern Territory and South Australia to western Queensland and New South Wales.

This species is very closely related to E. linearis (see Notes under that species). Although E. duttonii is a very distinct species it is very variable vegetatively. Spencer Moore based his E. calycina on a form common in the Flinders Ranges, which characteristically has shorter pedicels and broader leaves that are frequently more densely aggregated towards the branch apices. This form extends beyond the Flinders Ranges and gradually grades into the more widespread form with leaves scattered along the branches and longer, sigmoidally curved pedicels. The dense aggregation of leaves towards the branch tips may correlate with dryer, more exposed rocky situations where growth rate is slower and internodal length between leaves suppressed. The leaves of E. duttonii are normally entire but in a small number of collections, particularly from the Flinders Ranges (including the type of E. calycina S. Moore), they are serrulate. Often the margins of other leaves on the same plant are entire.

Eremophila eriocalyx is vegetatively a very uniform species, however, considerable variation occurs in corolla colour. Eremophila physocalyx is closely related to E. eriocalyx (see Notes under that species). The illustration of E. eriocalyx done by Graff (Mueller, 1886) is consistent with the species except for features of the flower. The corolla does not posess the typical 'closed throat' of this species and it is shown to have exserted stamens. Furthermore, the dissected corolla does not appear to be woolly inside and is clearly glabrous outside. I suspect therefore that the flower used in preparing the illustration did not belong to E. eriocalyx but probably got mixed in with the material, which has been found to be the case in other species illustrated by Graff

Eremophila forrestii is closely allied to E. glandulifera. See Notes under that species. Mueller based E. forrestii on a very fragmentary specimen with an immature flower in which the anthers had not yet become exserted so it is understandable why it was not considered by Bentham (E. leucophylla), Mueller (E. turtonii), Diels (E xanthotricha) and Fitzgerald (E. hastieana) when describing their new species. I have selected the Milne collection of E. leucophylla held at Kew, mounted on the sheet with a Helms collection, as lectotype for that name. The second sheet held at Kew (vegetative) is considered a syntype as is the Melbourne collection. E. turtonii was based on a form with obovate, cuneate leaves and obovate sepals but there is a complete gradation between this form and typical E. forrestii. E. xanthotricha was presumably recognised largely by the fact that the hairs on young growth were golden-yellow. However, this feature is of little significance as populations such as one examined south of Overlander Roadhouse (Chinnock 3794) consisted of a mixture of goldenand grey-haired forms with an approximate ratio of 1:1. Golden-haired forms appear to occur sporadically in many grey-tomentose species, including E. margarethae, E. latrobei and E punicea, but the condition is rare and it is usually confined to the young growth. In one species, E. citrina, it is the normal condition with grey-leaved forms being very rare. Barlow (1971) distinguished his E. sp. 2 from E. forrestii on the basis of its glabrous corolla, sessile flowers, valvate calyx-segments and larger leaves, gradually attenuated towards the base; however, this form is very close to the type of E. leucophylla and the corolla, like the fragmentary one present on the type specimen of E. forrestii, is not glabrous but obscurely glandular-pubescent. The imbrication of the sepals is also very variable. In E. forrestii subsp. forrestii they may be either valvate or imbricate in the upper part, whereas in E. forrestii subsp. hastieana they are imbricate to the base.

Eremophila galeata is most closely related to E. fraseri and initially I treated it as a subspecies of this species; however, the distinctive modified dorsal sepal with prominent ridged margins which, at the bud stage, overlap and enclose the anterior and inner sepals, the prominently laterally compressed flower bud, the prominently pubescent vegetative parts and pedicels, and the tetraploid chromosome state clearly distinguish this species from E. fraseri. This species is much more variable than E. fraseri. The leaves are usually lanceolate, gradually tapering into a winged petiole, but the leaf shape approaches E. fraseri on the northern limits of its range. Unlike E. fraseri, the margins are normally prominently undulate. Flower colour and spotting is also more variable. Like E. fraseri, the corolla tube is brown but the colour of the lobes may be off-white, whitish lilac, yellowish grey to carmine, with spotting varying greatly in distribution and density with some forms almost lacking spots. The hairs on the branches and leaves are usually immersed in the thick resin layer but they are usually evident on young growth at branch apices, towards leaf bases, and often visible through the translucent resin. On its northern limits where the species overlaps with E. fraseri, some intergrading may occur. The posterior sepal is not strongly modified like in southern populations and the ridging may only be evident near the apex of the sepal. The pubescent branches and leaves will, however, readily distinguish E. galeata.

Eremophila gibbosa is most closely related to E. virens. The corolla of E. virens is densely eglandular-pubescent outside, the hairs crisped, while E. gibbosa has a sparsely pubescent corolla except on the lobes. Eremophila gilesii is an extremely widespread species and is very variable in vegetative and floral features. Queensland and New South Wales populations of E. gilesii subsp. gilesii, disjunct from central and western populations, are tetraploid and morphologically relatively uniform. The type sheet contains elements of two forms of E. glabra. The upper part of the sheet contains six branch portions which agree best with the type description in having narrow elliptic, entire, leaves and tomentose branches. Although these six specimens appear to represent portions of the same plant or gathering, Brown did refer to three localities, although only two distinct collections can be recognised on the type sheet. In view of this I have selected as lectotype the specimen on the left-hand side of the 'type specimen' label. The other five specimens are designated isolectotypes. The lower half of the sheet contains four branch portions of a form of E. glabra common on the western coastal portions of Eyre Peninsula and the adjacent offshore islands. This form has broad obovate, almost glabrous leaves which have entire margins or with a few teeth towards the apex. The treatment of subspecies below is considered a tentative subdivision of this polymorphic species. Much more research needs to be undertaken on populations, especially in Western Australia, to resolve the many taxonomic problems associated with this super species. Although the nine subspecies treated here will account for much of the variation it is acknowledged that some plants will not fit easily into any subspecies and these may represent additional taxa that are not recognised. Furthermore, intergrades between subsp. glabra and subsp. albicans, subsp. albicans and subsp. elegans, subsp. albicans and subsp. tomentosa are known in Western Australia, and in the Murray Region of South Australia, for example, unusual forms are occasionally encountered which resemble in many ways forms of subsp. albicans and E. subfloccosa. The Eremophila glabra complex consisting of E. glabra, E. subfloccosa, E. decipiens, E. hilli, E. veneta, E. subteretifolia and E. splendens is a group of very closely related species, many of which appear to be undergoing a process of active speciation. In E. glabra, for example, over small distances, especially in the south-western part of Western Australia, it is quite possible to find very distinct morphological forms from prostrate, creeping shrubs to erect intricate shrubs with yellow, green or red flowers and leaves ranging from almost glabrous to tomentose.

Eremophila glabra subsp. albicans is common throughout the South-West Botanical Province of Western Australia. The typical form of this subspecies occurs in coastal regions from Shark Bay to Bunbury and along the southern coast to near Cape Arid. It is characterised by having very minute stellate hairs less than 0.1 mm across on the vegetative parts. These hairs are only obvious towards the branch tips and especially in the dried state give the immature leaves a mealy appearance, whereas in older leaves the hairs are scattered or lost. In this form the flowers are orange-red or yellow and appear to vary in colour within some populations (R.J. Cranfield 359) A second inland form, which occurs throughout the Avon and Roe Botanical Districts, and has a few scattered records in the Austin Botanical District, may represent a second taxon. It differs in having narrower leaves and much larger, interlacing stellate hairs on the vegetative parts. More commonly the branches, leaves, pedicels and sepals are tomentose. The leaves may be entire or toothed and the flower colour variable from red to yellowish green. George Bentham's E. glabra var. viridiflora was based on a yellowish green flower form of this type. There also appears to be differences in fruit structure between the coastal and inland forms; however, although a large number of collections were examined relatively few were fruiting so I cannot be certain as to the consistency of fruit differences. Coastal forms have subglobular to globular fruits, which appear quite fleshy. In contrast the inland form has an ovoid, slightly fleshy fruit, which is constricted distally with a shallow furrow between the two carpels.

The type of Eremophila graciliflora was collected by Oldfield near 'Yattoo' on the Murchison River, as was the type material of E. oldfieldii, and both species were described by Mueller in Fragmenta 1 on the same page. In the protologue of E. graciliflora, Mueller gave measurements for the sepals 'circiter 3" metientia' (ca 6 mm long). He further stated 'Drupa deficit'. However, in 3 of the 4 syntypes held at Melbourne, MEL 77683, 77684 and 77685, there are mixtures of calyces and/or mature fruit representing two species. In one collection, MEL 77684, a small packet labelled E. graciliflora in Mueller's hand has numerous large calyces with segments 18--20 mm long (= 9--10 lines) and a number of fruits, one of which is cut in half. There are also opened-out corollas, and this material appears to have been used by Graff (1886) for his illustration of E. graciliflora. A mature fruit was illustrated and a fruiting calyx was added to a branch. This illustration of E. graciliflora is considered to be a mixture of two species, E. graciliflora and E. oldfieldii. Of the four syntypes of E. graciliflora that had been isolated at Melbourne, two of them, MEL 77683 and 77685, are wholly material of E. oldfieldi and a third, MEL 77684, contains three branches of E. graciliflora, but the packets contain a mixture of leaves and flowers of this species and fruiting calyces and fruit of E. oldfieldii. There is no suggestion on any of the branches of E. graciliflora (MEL 77686) that these large fruiting calyces were ever attached even though Graff illustrated one as having been so. It seems likely that material of E. oldfieldii was mixed in with E. graciliflora after Mueller had prepared his description of E. graciliflora and that subsequently Graff prepared the illustration based on the material at his disposal or inadvertently mixed up plant material from different collections. In his protologue, Mueller gave size measurements of sepals which are consistent with flowering calyces of E. graciliflora and not the fruiting ones of E. oldfieldii. I have therefore, excluded the two sheets MEL 77683 and 77685 (wholly E. oldfieldii) from the type material of E. graciliflora and likewise the fruiting calyces and fruit in the packet attached to MEL 77684. It is possible that this material of E. oldfieldii represents part of the type gathering of this species, which was also collected from near 'Yattoo', presumably at the same time. It seems likely that E. graciliflora is a hybrid between E. Longifolia and E. oldfieldii. In the flowers examined, the anthers had not matured nor had they become exserted as would be expected for an ornithophilous species. In addition to this, vegetative and foral features appear intermediate between the two putative parents. The more dense, persistent indumentum, with many of the hairs more or less appressed, approaches E. longifolia. The straight pedicel, which is about 10mm long, contrasts with the shorter straight one of E. longifolia and the long sigmoidally curved one of E. oldfieldii. The sepal size is also intermediate and the corolla has scattered hairs outside similar to the type found in E. longifolia (E. oldfieldii is glabrous), while the corolla lobes and their dissection resembles more closely E Longifolia.

Eremophila longifolia is allied to E. laanii, differing in the indumentum of the stem and leaves, the size of the leaves, the pubescent corolla and the fruit. The widespread occurrence of this species over a broad range of climatic conditions and soil types has undoubtedly contributed to its variability. Although E. longifolia is a very well-defined species, which is unlikely to be confused with any all glandular. other, within the species there is considerable variation in the type and distribution of the indumentum, the habit of the plant and portion of outer surface of one sepal; B - F, sepal variants: B - C and to a lesser extent the leaf shape and sepal size. The variation in indumentum is obviously linked with aridity and in general central Australian forms have hoary leaves and stems, but in some cases (Gittens 2448, NSW) the branches, pedicels, sepals and bases of leaves have longer yellowish villous hairs. In Queensland and New South Wales, except in the western parts, and in south-eastern South Australia and Victoria the leaves are normally sparsely pubescent with scattered appressed obscure hairs on one surface and short erect glandular hairs on the other. This upper/lower surface distribution of hair types is marked in some cases (Dunlop 1092, CBG) while in other cases it becomes less marked with mixed glandular and appressed hairs equally distributed on both surfaces. In other cases Dunlop 1158, CBG) the majority of hairs on both surfaces are glandular with an absence of appressed hairs. The desert forms, although usually clothed in appressed greyish hairs, also possess obscure glandular hairs and these can (Gittens 2448), like eastern forms, have a dorsiventral pattern of distribution although much denser. A similar variation in the hairs on the branches can be found and in rare cases (C. Dunlop 1158, CBG) the hairs are The habit of the species also varies considerably. In desert forms the plant is usually a shrub or small tree but with the ability to root-sucker, resulting frequently in dense groups. However, in western New South Wales it often forms a solitary tree and root-suckering does not appear to occur. Unlike E. latrobei, in which the two known polyploid states have associated morphological differences which readily distinguish them, the diploid and tetraploid forms of E. Longifolia appear to be indistinguishable, although it is possible that a correlation may exist between leaf and corolla size and the polyploid state, with the diploid possessing smaller vegetative and floral parts. This situation, however, cannot be resolved until a more thorough survey of the Western Australian region is made, where forms similar to known diploid collections occur in the Yalgoo region but their polyploid level is unknown. In a number of collections (Copley 2899, AD; Gittens 2448, NSW; Sikkes 1296, CBG) hairs occur on the ovary and fruit. The occurrence of hairs on the ovary (fruit) appears to occur sporadically but there does not appear to be any correlation with any other feature and in itself is not considered sufficient to warrant recognition. The three collections cited above, for example, are from widely separated localities, namely Bute (SA), Mongrel Downs (NT) and MacCullochs Range (NSW), respectively. Eremophila longifolia is the only species in the genus exhibiting cauliflory and well-developed ramiflory. Another species, E. ramiflora, is also ramiflorous but this has resulted from the suppression of flower buds which had originally developed at the branch tips. Two species in sect. Virides, E. virens and E gibbosa, produce flowers from buds which develop at the end of the previous flowering season. In this case the new buds grow to about 2 mm diameter and then become dormant, recommencing development in autumn. In E. longifolia, floral initials can continue to develop each year on the older branches and it is not uncommon to find leafless thick woody branches with dense clusters of flowers and fruits. Flowers have also developed on the lower trunk of a 13- year-old, 4.5 m tall tree cultivated at Hendon; however, this appears to be uncommon.

Ewart and Davies (1917) based their E. macdonnellii var. macrocarpa on a mixture of E. macdonnellii and E. maculata, however, as most of their protologue refers to E. maculata I have lectotypified this name upon the Melbourne collection of E. maculata (MEL 83173). Eremophila madonnelli is extremely variable with respect to the type of indumentum and its distribution on the branches, leaves and calyx, the shape and size of the leaves, the pedicel length and the shape, size and arrangement of the calyx-lobes. Although there are a number of well-defined forms found in cultivation, when one examines the whole range of variation these distinctions are not maintained and as a consequence no subspecific taxa are recognised. At one extreme, the indumentum of the branches, leaves, pedicel and calyx is a fine grey-white tomentum of substellate-dendritic hairs (Chinnock 5552, Latz 4402) and at the other, plants are almost glabrous with only scattered short glandular and long eglandular hairs found on the branches and leaves, and short glandular and stellate hairs restricted to the margins of the calyx lobes (Latz 7489). Most plants have an indumentum of substellate-dendritic hairs interspersed with short, brown-tipped, glandular and longer setaceous eglandular ones, variable in density and combination. Leaf shape and size is also very variable, ranging from narrow linear, acute, leaves 35 x 2--3 mm (Latz 7489) to ovate or obovate, obtuse ones as small as 4 × 2 mm (Bloods Creek, S.A. White s.n., AD 97620008). The arrangement and shape of the calyx-lobes on the tube is also variable. The lobes may be similar in size and more or less equally arranged on the rim (Chinnock 5552) or unequally arranged with 3, usually smaller, posterior lobes, and 2 anterior ones (Barlow 1132).

Eremophila maculata is one of the most widespread species in the genus. The structure of the flower is relatively uniform within the species with the exception of the colour and spotting. This can be extremely variable within and between populations of subsp. maculata. The shape of the leaf, however, is very variable and it is largely on this feature that the three subspecies are distinguished E. maculata subsp. maculata, widespread throughout the eastern and central States, is replaced in Western Australia, except in the Kimberley area and along the Nullarbor, by subsp. brevifolia, a smaller often divaricate shrub with distinctly petiolate, elliptic, obovate or suborbicular leaves. In this subspecies the flower is less variable in colour and commonly carmine and without spotting. In subsp. maculata flower colour varies through carmine, brick-red, brownish red to pure yellow and occasionally bluish purple. The flowers are usually prominently spotted within the tube or on the lobes, although in some yellow forms the spotting is absent. Spotting can vary greatly within a population. Within subsp. maculata there is considerable variation in the degree of tomentum on the branches and in the shape of the leaf. In the extreme northern part of it range, extending from the Kimberley in Western Australia through the Northern Territory to Queensland, plants consistently have narrower leaves than elsewhere. This form of subsp. maculata approaches subsp. filifolia and is probably more closely allied to it than subsp. brevifolia. Ewart and Davies (1917) based E. macdonnellii var. macrocarpa on a mixture of E. macdonnellii and E. maculata; however, most of their account refers to E. maculata so I have lectotypified this name on the Melbourne collection of E. maculata (MEL 83173), which consists of a packet containing numerous fruits and loose leaves. Hill's collection (GH 347) cited in the protologue is referrable to E. macdonnellii.

Eremophila margarethae is a widespread, relatively uniform, common species, which is often very dominant in the shrub layer. It is easily identified by the grey vegetative parts which often appear pseudoglabrous because the fine stellate tomentum enveloped with resin which, when dry, results in the individual hairs becoming indistinct and the surface appearing more or less glabrous. Anther distinctive feature of this species is the very narrow linear-triangular to lanceolate, blackish purple, rarely green, sepals, which are usually visible through the dense hair layer. Occasionally very narrow-leaved forms 1--1.5 mm wide are encountered (Chinnock 8067) but typically the leaf width is 2.5--4 mm. This species is susceptible to Hopbush soft scale (Pulvinaria dodonaeae) and Richmond (pers. comm. 1993) found that 10 per cent the population of E. margarethae at one site on Mt Weld Station, south-west of Laverton, was killed by this insect.

It grows on duplex soils, clays, earths and sands and forms a major component of most woodlands, and invades pastureland. A detailed account of the ecology and control of this species is provided by Beeston and Webb (1977). It is common in a variety of vegetation communities including brigalow (Acacia harpophylla), wilga (Geijera parvifolia), belah (Casuarina cristata), gidgee (Acacia cambagei), mulga (Acacia aneura), white cypress pine (Callitris glaucophylla), leopard wood (Flindersia maculosa) and tumble box (Eucalyptus populnea).

Eremophila mitchellii is very close to E. sturtii and it is often difficult to distinguish between these two species. Smith (1975) separated the two on the basis of flower colour, corolla pubescence and leaf shape and although these are very useful characters none of them are absolute. Two features found to be consistently different were the number of flowers in the axil, and the bark. The bark of E. mitchellii is only shallowly fissured and flakes into small pieces with the basal part of each piece curling outwards. In E. sturtii, if a trunk is formed, the bark is thick, firm and deeply fissured. Normally there is a solitary flower in the axil of E. sturtii although sometimes an odd branch will produce paired flowers while.in E. mitchellii there are two or three flowers in each axil. Sometimes in E. mitchelli only one flower develops although the aborted second (and third) bud is always visible. In most cases flower colour and pubescence will distinguish between the two species. The outside of the floral tube of E. mitchelli is very sparsely obscurely glandular-puberulent to almost glabrous and the corolla white, although, very rarely, pink to mauve forms do occur (Muffet MS/329, CBG). In contrast, the corolla tube of E. sturtii is densely pubescent, mauve to pinkish mauve in colour or, more rarely, almost white. Considerably more variation was found in the indumentum of the ovary and fruit of E. mitchellii than reported by Smith (1975). Although the fruit is commonly densely villous with numerous shorter glandular hairs, the longer villous hairs may become very scattered or absent with the fruit being only glandular-pubescent. In populations adjacent to the coast in the Townsville region the ovary is completely glabrous (Chinnock 5834, AD; Lazarides & Storey 35, CANB). The fruit type in E. sturtii is uniform over its range. The timber of E. mitchelli is fine grained and often called rosewood. It is also scented and has been exported to China in the past as an incense substitute. It is a light wood but very tough and resistant to white ants (Anderson, 1968). Rabbits freely eat the bark when other food sources are scarce, and twigs and bark have been used with strychnine for poison bait (Anderson, 1968).

In his original account of the species, Black cited two collections from Macumba, South Australia, and between Crown Point and Horseshoe Bend, Finke River, immediately after the Latin diagnosis and followed this by a comment on the flowering period. These two collections are thus interpreted as syntypes. In further discussion on the species, specimens in Schomburg's herbarium and a collection made by Miss Staer were also mentioned, and these are considered paratypes. The two syntypes and part of the collection made by Miss Staer are mounted on one sheet and they have associated with them numerous notes and sketches made by Black. The Macumba collection is selected here as lectotype since it is the most complete, consisting of branches, leaves and flowers. This species is most closely related to E. viscida Endl. and E. lucida, sharing a similar flower structure with obtuse corolla lobes and an emarginate lower lobe. It differs from these species in having densely pubescent possessing branched hairs and normally a glabrous fruit. Eremophila neglecta is a relatively uniform species with respect to its vegetative and most of its floral features. Although the gynoecium is glabrous in the great majority of cases, a few specimens have been noted in which either the cm 1￾8 mm. style or ovary or both possess eglandular hairs. The density and distribution of these hairs was found to be quite variable. Two collections, Brooks 4 (AD) and Ising s.n. (AD 97309292), have a considerable vestige of hair on the distal part of the ovary and basal part of the style while in other specimens, Chinnock 425 and Weber 254, the ovary possessed only one or a few hairs in the distal part while the style was either sparsely hirsute in the lower third or possessed one to a few very scattered hairs in the lower half. E. neglecta is the only species in section Pulchrisepalae with branched hairs.

Eremophila oppositifolia possesses one of the least specialised ornithophilous flower types. The corolla lobes are broad, obtuse and similar in size although the upper pair are fused for most of their length. The stamens are exerted to the tip of the upper pair of lobes or just beyond them. These features, together with the large sepals, suggest that E. oppositifola is closely allied to E. platycalyx subsp. pardalota. It differs from E. platycalyx in the size and shape of the leaves, the absence of spotting on the corolla, and the size and shape of the fruit. Subsp. angustifolia is the common taxon throughout Western Australia. Typically it forms a tall shrub or small tree with a rounded crown. The leaves are typically terete, oppositely arranged and usually short, straight and rigid, never becoming Alexuose as in the type subspecies. In the extreme north-western part of its range, leaves are flattened as they are in subsp. rubra. The flower, as in the type subspecies, is typically cream tinged pink above, although one striking variant was found in a population east of Dallwallinu. In this population many individuals possessed flowers with dark maroon sepals and corollas while others had the normal colour form with cream sepals. Many intermediate colour shades were also present. Over most of its range the type subspecies forms a straggly shrub rarely approaching tree proportions. The leaves are opposite, flexible and flexuose. The leaves are typically flattened on the upper side and slightly folded so that they are distinctly channelled above. In the north-western and south-eastern parts of the range of this subspecies, intergrades with subsp. angustifolia (north-west) and subsp. rubra (south-east) occur. There is no question that the different collections of E. oppositifola made near Emu, Great Victoria Desert, belong to subsp. angustifolia and some populations in the Gawler Ranges are perhaps best included under this subspecies. However, in the Gawler Ranges and Eyre Peninsula, subterete forms approach subsp. angustifolia but in these cases some leaves are usually broader and flatter and all are distinctly flattened on the upper side. Along the South Australian border and adjacent regions in Victoria and New South Wales from Broken Hill southwards forms of subsp. oppositifolia approach subsp. rubra.

This very common species is extremely adaptable, occurring on calcareous loams, red-brown sandy or clay loams on the plains or on breakaways and stony rises or on hills. Eremophila pantonii is a very uniform species with the exception of the flower and leaf length and the density of leaves. In some populations the flower is extremely large (25--30 mm) and the leaves larger and more distinctly spaced, while in other populations the leaves are densely clustered and the flowers less than 20mm, however, these are considered extremes. For a given population the plants are relatively uniform. In most areas E. pantonii is easily distinguished from the other species in this section by its alternate leaves but in the occasional case when the leaves are oppositely arranged it can be distinguished by the large scattered tubercles on the branches.

Eremophila parvifolia is related to E. weldii, differing in its divaricate habit, smaller leaves, glandular pubescence, differently coloured flower and by its subglobular to conical fruit. Although in most cases subsp. auricampa is a more erect non-spinescent shrub (Kalgoorlie region), a population at Lake Cowan (Chinnock 5461) was spinescent and low growing, consistent in habit with the type subspecies. The two subspecies are, however, readily distinguished by the shape of the fruit and the presence or virtual absence of hairs on the ovary and fruit. One specimen of subsp. parvifolia collected by the Pastoral Board of South Australia north of Hughes is distinct from other South Australian collections in that the branches and leaves are densely eglandular-pubescent with numerous shorter glandular hairs. The sepals are also eglandular-pubescent outside. In the absence of flowers and the vague locality data no attempt has been made to distinguish this form here. A collection of subsp. auricampa also has pubescent branches, leaves and calyces (G. Barrett s.n., PERTH) but in addition the leaves are much larger, up to 9 × 6 mm with a distinct petiole.

Eremophila platycalyx is an extremely polymorphic species, especially with respect to leaf shape and the shape and spotting of the corolla. Broad-leaved forms of the species are largely concentrated in the eastern part of the species range, and it is considered that Kraenzlin (1929) based his species E dielsiana (type destroyed) on this form. Furthermore, Kraenzlin's E. platycalyx var. Lancifolia described on the same paper was also based on this broad-leaved form but in this case he did not appear to have seen any dried material, merely describing the variety upon the top right-hand figure depicted in Graff's illustration of E. platycalyx in Mueller's 'Myoporinous Plants of Australia' (1866). Although extreme narrow- and broad-leaved forms of E. platycalyx appear very distinct, complete intergrading between these forms occurs. The flowers within a population of subsp. platycalyx may be uniform or vary markedly from plant to plant although for an individual the corolla form is constant. The cream corolla may be prominently spotted blackish purple outside with the anthers commonly exserted to the throat or just beyond the lobes of the upper lip, or it may be unspotted, in which case the anthers are enclosed within the throat. In subsp. pardalota the corolla is uniformly narrow tubular, prominently spotted outside and the stamens exserted to the lobes of the upper lip. This is the only species of Eremophila showing floral adaptations to both ornithophily and entomophily within different populations with many intermediate stages.

The similar vegetative features of E. fraseri, E. galeata, E. flaccida and E. ramiflora largely explain why the three latter species were overlooked for such a long time. One must acknowledge, however, that collections of these latter species have been totally inadequate and this is probably due to the fact that E. fraseri sens. lat., being so common and widespread, had not been collected with discretion. Unlike E. fraseri, E. galeata and E. flaccida, the flower colour of E. ramiflora is carmine and the sepals, also carmine, are subequal. At all the populations that I studied E. ramiflora there was no variation at all in the colour intensity of the calyx and corolla, only in the prominence of the spotting. In this species, flower buds develop in leaf axils of new growth; however, often buds are suppressed and may remain dormant for one or more years before developing further. This results in flowers frequently occurring a considerable way back down the stem amongst old dead leaves or leaf base remnants. This may be a method of conserving energy by bud suppression when conditions turn unfavourable. Bud suppression in E. ramiflora is comparable with that occurring in E. virens and E. gibbosa where the following year's flower buds develop to a certain stage towards the end of the season when fruits are developing and then go dormant until the following autumn.

Eremophila rotundifolia is extremely widespread in central South Australia throughout the Gairdner- Torrens Region, extending into the western part of the Lake Eyre Basin Region. There are two records from the North-Western Region and one record from the Northern Territory. This species usually occurs on stony tablelands and hard-pan gibber plains, on desert loams with mulga, Senna and Eremophila spp. or in grassland with bluebush.

The lectotype at MEL is very fragmentary consisting of a few loose leaves and flower fragments. The Kew isolectotype consists of an long portion of branch with leaves but lacking flowers. I have selected the MEL collection because it is more complete in having both leaves and flowers. This species is very closely allied to E. spathulata W. V. Fitzg Both species possess a silvery-grey tomentum on the branches and leaves, and a similar corolla, however, the leaf bases of E. rotundifolia are not concurrent with the branches, the branches are prominently tuberculate, the sepals are subequal, and the leaves are generally shorter and broader. Eremophila rotundifolia is relatively uniform over its range, however, two collections from Anna Creek (Milthorpe 3050, Lothian 1351) differ in having longer petioles, ovate leaves with acute apices and flowers on pedicels 15--35 mm long. This form most probably represents a distinct subspecies, which approaches in leaf form E. spathulata; however, further material is required before this can be determined.

Eremophila santalina usually forms a small tree with weak drooping branches, although at the shrub stage the branches are erect and it can be easily mistaken for either E. deserti or E. fallax; however, the thinner leaves which are attenuated to both base and apex and the larger, smooth, shiny brown fruit readily distinguish this species. In his protologue account of Pholidiopsis santalina, Mueller provided descriptions of flowers and fruit including measurements. Mueller collected this species at Cudnaka but of the three herbarium sheets attributed to Mueller held at MEL, there is only one that has a direct reference to this locality. This sheet (MEL 77714) has a small portion of vegetative branch and two associated labels. One white label in Mueller's hand has 'Pholidiopsis santalina Ferd. Mueller, Myoporinae' at the top, followed by a description of the plant which continues on to the other side of the label. This description gives details of flowers and at the bottom there is reference to Cudnaka and a date of Oct. 51, followed by Eremophila santalina and Dr M, indicating that he was the collector. The other two collections that appear to be part of this gathering are consistent with the Cudnaka specimen and have labels in Mueller's hand. One sheet (MEL 83702) has two associated labels, one pink with Pholidiopsis santalina written in Mueller's hand and the other blue, which originally formed part of one of Mueller's small folded packets, commonly made to enclose fragments or dissected flowers, and has Eremophila santalina written on it. Both these labels have been initialled by Bentham. This specimen has buds and one fruit. The other sheet, MEL 83701, has two large portions of branch possessing flowers with corollas, and a cellophane bag with fragments including one fruit. There is a label in Mueller's hand with 'n.g. Pholidiopsis santalina Ferd Mueller, N. Holl. Austr. interior, Ferd Mueller'. According to Grandison (1990), Mueller visited the Flinders Ranges only once and as he would have been limited in what he could collect and carry, it is reasonable to assume that he made one gathering of Pholidiopsis santalina and that the three specimens at MEL, attributed to Mueller, are part of the one collection. Certainly Mueller's protologue description could not have been based upon the 'Cudnaka' specimen, as it is vegetative. Mueller had a habit of providing different wording on labels of what appear to be duplicates and according to Dr J. Ross (pers. comm.), it is not unusual to find no label that bears the precise wording provided by Mueller in his protologue. I have therefore lectotypified upon the most complete specimen possessing flowers and fruits (MEL 83701) and the other two sheets are considered syntypes.

No other material of this species appears to have been collected until May 1994 when Mrs Mary Hancock forwarded me a small pressed specimen she had found near Moora the previous year. Both species have leaves in whorls and longitudinally ribbed branches, however, E. scaberula is distinguished from this species by the smaller flattened scaberulous leaves, the presence of stellate hairs (although usually obscured by resin) on the branches and leaves, the very short pedicels and the smaller flowers. One feature of this species is the ability to defoliate during prolonged dry periods and when in this condition confirmation can usually be made by searching under the shrub and finding the fruits. Eremophila spuria is extremely widespread throughout the Austin Botanical District and also extends into the adjacent portion of the Ashburton Botanical District, Western Australia. Eremophila spuria superficially resembles a number of species including E. granitica, E. hughesii and narrow-leaved forms of E. clarkei; however, it is closely related to E. hughesii and E. setacea. These three species possess a characteristic swollen sepal apex, most pronounced in E. spuria, which distinguishes them from forms of E. clarkii and E. granitica. E. spuria is distinguished from E. setacea by the prominently glandular-pubescent sepals, the more resinous leaves and branches and the usually more slender leaves' and from E. hughesii by the nonweeping habit and obtuse corolla lobes. Eremophila spuria often occurs on sand plain as localised very dense stands and it has been noted that plants in these populations all appear to be of a similar age. Eremophila subfloccosa is very close to E. glabra but differs in consistently having yellow or green flowers, erect, imbricate leaves and the branches and leaves (at least towards the base) possessing long lax white branched hairs. It is also aromatic. Although E. subfloccosa was described by Bentham in 1870, this species did not appear in Mueller's lithographs of Myoporinous Plants of Australia published in 1886. There is, however, a drawing at the National Herbarium of Victoria which was obviously done by Graff for the book. The outline and arrangement of the leaves appear to have been based on the type (MEL), but the flowers are not consistent with either Bentham's protologue or the type. The one bud present on the type is stenochiloid (ornithophilous) whereas the flowers illustrated are of an entomophilous form. Mueller obviously had doubts about the accuracy of the flower drawings and in his handwriting at the top he wrote, 'Eremophila subfloccosa sect. Platychilus sect. Stenochilus', and at the bottom of the page he commented 'flowers blue, not a stenochilos according to the drawing which may be wrong. It seems likely that because of these doubts Mueller excluded the species from his book.

In structure the fruit of E. tetraptera is subschizocarpic. At maturity the fruit splits medially along the four wings across the fruit between the two carpels and at right angles to this between the two locules of each carpel, resulting in four fruit segments with each segment formed by the portion of two adjacent wings and a locule. Although the four segments are well defined they normally do not completely separate. The leaves have a well-defined abscission layer and separate cleanly from the branch leaving a pronounced leaf scar. The relationships of E. tetraptera with other species in the genus are obscure.

Eremophila tietkensii is extremely widespread in the Ashburton, Fortesque, Canning, Carnegie and +20 Giles Botanical Districts where it grows along drainage channels on sandy clay loams or on stony slopes of lateritic rises and small hills. It is usually associated with species of Acacia and Eremophila.

In 1975, L.S. Smith lectotypified E. tietkensii upon a specimen held at MEL collected by W. Tietkens in 1899 at Mt Sonder during an expedition exploring and prospecting the MacDonnell Ranges. In the protologue of E. tietkensii, Mueller and Tate merely gave the location for this new species as 'Central Australia' but elsewhere in the paper, in a list of plants collected on the expedition, two locations, Lara Vale and Mt Sonder, were given. From the collections held at MEL and AD it is clear that Mueller and Tate had different concepts of what was E. tietkensii (Chinnock, in press), with Tate annotating specimens from Mt Sonder as E. tietkensii (all E. latrobei), while similar specimens seen by Mueller were identified as E. latrobei. There is one specimen held at MEL, collected at Lara Vale and annotated by Mueller as E. tietkensii, which is consistent with the protologue of E. tietkensii, unlike the Mt Sonder material, so this specimen is treated as the holotype. Eremophila tietkensii is closely allied to E. platycalyx and E. macmillaniana but is easily distinguished from these species by having 2--4 flowers in the axils and numerous branches arising from near ground level. Commonly the corolla of E. tietkensii is pale lilac or white tinged lilac and very rarely it may be purple spotted on the outside. Although the leaves are typically long and lanceolate in form, very small forms do occur in the north-western part of the species range and may represent a distinct subspecies.

Eremophila viscida is restricted to the Irwin, Avon and Roe (extreme north-western part) Botanical Districts of Western Australia. It is known from scattered localities in the wheat belt extending from Ballidu and Latham in the north-west to Westonia and Merredin in the south-east. It grows on light brown sandy and clay loams over granites or red-brown clay loams in the north-western part of its range. It is usually associated with Acacia spp. It is rarely common and often occurs as a few scattered individuals along roadsides.

Eremophila viscida is closely allied to both E. neglecta and E. lucida, differing from the former in having glabrous branches, longer, glabrous, shiny leaves, the colour of the sepals and corolla and the pubescent fruit; and from the latter by the flower colour, shorter pedicels, terete or obscurely ribbed branches and the glandular-pubescent outer corolla surface. Two distinct colour forms occur in this species. The calyx can be cream tinged metallic blue-green and the corolla cream with blackish purple spots, or the calyx is pinkish carmine and the corolla cream tinged carmine with carmine blotches or lines. Originally it appeared that the former colour form was restricted to the Latham region; however, both colour forms have been found in a number of populations north-east of Merredin with no intermediates observed. This species appears to be relatively short-lived and tall plants are very prone to stems collapsing at ground level. Whether this is the result of inability to support the weight of branches or insect damage of the stems at ground level has not been determined.

This species occurs on brown clay or sandy loams in the areas around Ravensthorpe and, at one locality SW of the town, the species occurred along a dry stream course on sandy, hard brown loams over granite in a Eucalyptus occidentalisl anceps/ foecunda woodland. In his prologue Mueller merely gave collection details as 'in rocky hills near to the Phillips River. Maxwell., and there were a number of collections in the Melbourne and Kew Herbaria, seen by George Bentham, that fit this information. Glycocystis has a very limited range and is largely concentrated in the areas to the south to south-west of Ravensthorpe through which the Phillips River passes. Although there are no Phillips Ranges in the southern part of Western Australia, I am of the opinion that this reference on the labels was to the 'ranges' in the vicinity of the Phillips River. There is no 'Eyres Relief' now recognised, but it is most likely that this name was used by Maxwell for the Eyre Ranges (which are at the most only low undulating hills). On all labels there is reference to either loose or decomposed limestone banks, sand flares, steep bluffs or rocky declivities, which agree with the protologue. I have selected as lectotype the Melbourne specimen that has Maxwell's name on a label, although there seems little doubt that the other collections are his also.

Myoporum acuminatum is closely allied to M. obscurum, M. insulare and M. montanum and extreme forms of the latter two species are often difficult to distinguish from it if not in flower or fruit. Like M. insulare, the sepals have thin membranous translucent marginal borders which are often irregularly toothed, and a dark purple to purplish black fruit, but it is readily distinguished from this species by the thinner elliptic leaves with a long attenuate apex, the larger, very prominently spotted flowers with exserted stamens and the diagnostic rugose ovary and fruit which it shares with M. obscurum. The rugose surface of the fruit is particularly obvious at immature stages. Myoporum montanum can be readily distinguished from M. acuminatum by the smaller, narrower leaves, sepals lacking expanded translucent margins, the smooth ovary and the pinkish purple to light purple smooth fruit. Juvenile plants (and probably regrowth shoots) may produce extremely large leaves and specimens collected at Batemans Bay (Chinnock 6653) were up to 275 x 66 mm.

Myoporum caprarioides is widespread along the coastal strip from the Greenough River mouth south to Busselton. It is commonly found on sandy or peaty soils in swampy situations, depressions or along watercourses. It is frequently associated with tuart forest (Eucalyptus gomphocephala), Melaleuca raphiophylla or in coastal heaths.

Myoporum caprarioides is closely allied to M. oppositifolium and replaces this species northwards along the coastal belt. It is readily distinguished from M. oppositifolium by its alternate leaves, which taper to a petiole-like base. It favours swampy situations whereas M. oppositifolium tends to grow in drier sites in sandy soils or on coastal cliffs. This species is quite variable and both M. gracile Bartling and M. serratum var. parvifforum Benth. were based on small leaf and flower forms respectively. Previously Myoporum subserratum Nees has been included in the synonymy of M. tetrandrum, and although I include it here in the synonymy of M. caprarioides, the type specimen has features to suggest that it is probably a hybrid between this species and M. insulare R. Br. The leaves fall within the size range of M. caprarioides rather than M. insulare and although most have the form of the former species, some leaves do have broader, more rounded apices more typical of the latter species. In addition the leaves are thicker and either entire or obscurely bluntly toothed, features of M. insulare. Although the anthers are long-exserted like M. caprarioides, the corolla lobes are obtuse, the pedicels short and thick and the sepals shorter and broader with slight membranous margins, all features associated with M. insulare.

The unique twiggy habit and leaf form of M. cordifolium makes it stand apart from the other species in the genus. The ontogeny of the leaf during seedling development does however suggest that the ancestral species from which M. cordifolium evolved had leaves similar to flattened forms found in section Disoon. Flower and fruit structure also support this link. and developing fruits Leaf development of a seedling (based on a number of seedlings) is as follows. The first two leaves (following cotyledons) are opposite, oblanceolate, obtuse, entire, 22 × 3 mm. Leaves 3 and 4 are subopposite, oblanceolate, acute and distinctly toothed in the distal half. They are slightly shorter than leaves 1 and 2 but broader, 20 x 5.5 mm. The fifth leaf is alternately arranged, oblanceolate, acute and irregularly coarsely toothed, with incurved teeth and the surface faintly tuberculate. It is half the length of the previous leaf, 10 × 3 mm. Leaf 6 is ovate-triangular, 6.5 × 3.5 mm. Leaves 7 to 9 gradually decrease in size and are more erect and incurving towards the branch, and by leaf 10 the adult form is attained. Variation in the number of leaves involved in the transition from juvenile to adult leaf is dependent on conditions, with vigorous, rapidly growing seedlings usually producing more juvenile leaves (AD 98951231). It was also noted that lateral shoots which developed in the leaf axils of the first leaf pair formed adult leaves immediately although the first two leaves were slightly larger and comparable with leaves 8 and 9 on the main axis. Germination of seed from freshly collected fruits is slow. Fruits sown in a pot (March 31, 1988) were buried just below the soil surface and regularly watered, but only one seedling had appeared by September of that year. In late September, the pot was removed from the glasshouse and placed outside in full sun. A rapid germination occurred at the beginning of May 1989, following relatively mild temperatures and good soaking rains, and 17 seedlings had appeared by May 4, 29 by May 17 and 61 by May 19. It would appear that this species, like many species of Eremophila, requires a period of weathering ( to high summer temperatures) before germination will occur. In the case of the population studied near Gairdner River (Chinnock 4942) it would appear that the species responds rapidly, especially in disturbed sites, to good autumnwinter rainfall, resulting in a rapid germination and seedling development with flowering occurring within 12--15 months. Plants at this population were numerous and appeared to be all of a similar age, suggesting a mass germination at the site. The species is thought to be short-lived.

Myoporum laetum is very readily distinguished from other species in the genus by the very numerous prominent pellucid spots (embedded resin vesicles), which are visible when leaves (fresh or dried) are held up to the light. It occurs on a wide variety of soil types from cracking clays, silty loams, loams derived from metamorphic, basaltic and calcareous rocks to sand plains, sand dunes, humus-rich soils along creeks in higher rainfall areas and rocky skeletal soils in mountain areas. In more arid areas M. montanum is restricted to drainage lines and creek beds in upland areas and it is frequently associated with Eucalyptus camaldulensis. It is also frequently encountered along the coast and in depression areas of flood plains. The species is also common on islands off the Queensland coast.

Myoporum montanum is an extremely variable, ubiquitous species within which three forms can be distinguished but because of inadequacies of dried herbarium material and the intergrades which link these forms I have refrained from recognising infraspecific taxa in this treatment. Detailed population studies, especially along the coastal areas of Queensland and northern New South Wales, will be necessary to determine consistency of morphological characters before a meaningful subdivision can be developed. The three forms that are recognised are discussed below: a) TYPE form - Robert Brown based the species on a narrow-leaved form found in the Blue Mountains. It is particularly common in the West Wyalong-Temora-Coolamon area. This form typically has narrow linear leaves 3--5 mm broad and small white unspotted or faintly spotted flowers, <8 mm in diameter. The flowers are bisexual or functionally dioecious. b) DESERT form - Throughout the arid areas of Western Australia, southern Northern Territory, South Australia, Queensland, New South Wales and along the Murray River in north-western Victoria occurs a form which forms a large shrub or small tree. It has thick linear-elliptic leaves in which the venation is obscured except for the basal part of the midrib. The flowers are bisexual, usually 10--15 mm in diameter, white and prominently spotted red-purple to purple. c) TROPICAL form - Extending along coastal and adjacent regions from Broome, across the north and down the eastern coast to northern New South Wales as well as in New Guinea and Timor is a form first recognised by Bentham (1870) as M. acuminatum var. parviflorum. This form has very small white unspotted flowers rarely reaching 8 mm in diameter. Unlike the Desert form this has thin leaves with obvious venation and discolorous surfaces although I am not certain whether the two surfaces are always discolorous. It would appear that in this form the flowers can be bisexual or functionally male or female. Populations studied near Ipswich were found at one site to consist of functionally female plants (R.J. Chinnock 8285) and at another a few kilometres away only bisexual plants (R.J. Chinnock 8284). As in Eremophila deserti, the male flowers are slightly larger with prominent anthers and a long style with an undeveloped stigmatic apex. Female flowers have small, undeveloped anthers and a short style with a large papillose stigmatic apex. It has also been noted in populations of M. insulare around Adelaide that frequently plants within populations may be functionally bisexual or female and it is suspected, from the examination of herbarium collections, that other species may vary from the normal bisexual condition too. Bloembergen (1951) referred to 4- and 6-lobed corollas in Malesian material, however, I have only noted 5-lobed ones in Australian populations although variations from 5 have been noted in other Australian species.

Myoporum sandwicense is extremely polymorphic, ranging from a low decumbent shrub to a small tree to 20 m with a trunk circumference of up to 0.9 m. Leaves are extremely variable in their shape, size, margin and pubescence. The flower parts range in number from 5--9 and fruits are variable in shape and can be smooth to prominently ribbed and have 5--12 locules. The two subspecies recognised here appear to have well-defined boundaries. Subsp. lanaiense has a quite unique lenticular fruit which readily distinguishes it, although immature fruits can sometimes be misleading as they more closely approach in shape forms found in subsp. sandwicense. Subsp. sandwicense is extremely variable, occurring on all main islands of the Hawaiian chain from sea level to over 3200 m, and growing in both dry and mesic habitats. I have included here forms previously recognised as var. fauriei (Lévl.) Webster and subsp. st johnii Webster. The former variety merely represents an extreme robust form of this subspecies, which is found at higher altitudes on Hawaii, and the latter, although it has a tendency to have more numerous floral parts and consistently possesses a hirsute style, overlaps in characters with forms found in other places. Indeed, although the hirsute style is virtually restricted to this form, a sparsely hirsute one has been noted in some collections of subsp. sandwicense from other islands (e.g. Chinnock 7846).
