Myoporum stellatum is restricted to the coral plain on the south-west corner of O'ahu between Pearl Harbour and Barbers Point although now extinct at many sites. There is one old record for Kaua'i Island, which is considered doubtful. It occurs on coralline sandy loams and at Kalaeoloa (Barbers) Point was associated with Hibiscus tiliaceus, Ipomea pes-caprae, Rhagodia semibaccata, Capparis, Lycium and Sporobolus.

Although M. stellatum has been treated as a variety of M. sandwicense, I am quite satisfied that it should be recognised at species level. It is more closely related to M degeneri, which has similar-structured glandular hairs although they are all simple. The simple or stellate to substellate indumentum found on the vegetative and floral parts of these two species is unique within the family, both in the colour and structure of the hairs. Although there are numerous branched hair types in Eremophila none appear analogous to those found in M. stellatum and M. degeneri. Although well-defined hairs are developed in other species of Myoporum, for example, M. sandwicense, M. crassifolium (sometimes), M. betcheanum, M. velutinum, these hairs are simple eglandular ones. Short glandular hairs may occasionally occur on sepal margins in these and other species and in M. betcheanum they are intermixed with longer eglandular hairs on vegetative parts, but these glandular hairs are consistent with types found in Eremophila. The development of the branched hairs in M. stellatum can be followed during seedling development (see Chinnock, AD 99508016). The cotyledons and hypocotyl of the seedling are prominently glandular-pubescent with all hairs simple as in M. degeneri. The first two leaves, which are oppositely arranged, have some simple glandular hairs but these are much shorter than those of the cotyledons and are largely confined to the margins in the distal part of the leaves. By the second leaf pair the glandular hairs have contracted to sessile glands and there is no evidence of any branched hairs. Successive leaves are alternately arranged with simple glandular hairs beginning to develop again on the stem and leaves, but by leaf 6, only branched hairs develop. Between leaf 8 and leaf 12, the branched hairs are few and scattered but most frequent along the midrib. The density and cover of branched glandular hairs gradually increases with successive leaves. Webster (1951) noted that the fifth stamen was often lost in this species; however, I noted in the Barbers Point population some corollas with 4 or 6 lobes, and with 1 or a number of non-functional stamens. Variations, particularly in the number of corolla lobes and stamen number, occur in other species apart from the Hawaiian ones-M. viscosum, for example, may have up to 8 lobes and 7 stamens and M. brevipes 4 lobes. In M. insulare quite often all 4 stamens are non-functional in a given flower, depending on when the flowers are produced. More irregularities appear to occur at the beginning or end of a flowering season.

Pentacoelium bontioides is restricted to coastal areas in southern Japan, including the Ryukyu Archipelago, and South China, including Taiwan and Hong Kong. It grows in mangrove situations along beaches at high tide line or along inlets and in coves free of strong wave or surf action. In Japan it is often associated with the sea-grass Zoysia sinica var. nipponica.

Toyoma and Itow (1975) reported that the fruit of this species is distributed by sea water. The cell structure in the outer layers of the endocarp of the fruit is similar to that found in Bontia daphnoides, which is also considered to be dispersed by this means. The Munich type appears to be the material upon which Siebold and Zuccarinii based Pentacoelium. In a small package are two cross-section portions of an immature fruit and an open corolla, which appear to be those depicted in Tab. 36 of their treatment. In the absence of other material I have treated the Munich specimen as the holotype. In the absence of a specimen in the De Candolle Herbarium, I have lectotypified P. chinense on the one held in the Paris Herbarium, as it is highly likely that De Candolle saw this material.
